225.title: Not by birth (383–390)
225.hook: not by birth is one a brahmana, but by conduct; cut the stream, be bold
225.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use the brahmana chapter and the Vasala Sutta to teach that worth comes from conduct, not birth; in Theravada countries the chapter's verses are often chanted, and its refrain is well known.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dahara, and your line: young and awake. Today, a new week, and the last chapter of the Dhammapada.

Old money. Good family. A title you inherit. Every society has words of honor that come with a family name. Yet a person with every advantage of birth can behave badly, and a person with none of them can be simply noble. The last chapter of the Dhammapada takes a word of honor from its world and asks a sharp question: what actually earns it? Verse after verse in it ends the same way.
screen: `WORDS OF HONOR BY BIRTH.` → `NOBLE WITHOUT ANY ADVANTAGE.` → `WHAT ACTUALLY EARNS IT?`

segments.voice: Today's word is brahmana, in Sanskrit brahmin. In the Buddha's India, brahmins were the hereditary priestly class, keepers of the Vedas and the sacred rites, and many were honored teachers; in the suttas, brahmins come to the Buddha as questioners, and some become his students. In these verses the word stays a word of honor. What changes is what it takes to earn it. In the discourse on the outcast, he puts it directly: no one is an outcast by birth, and no one is a brahmin by birth. By deeds one becomes an outcast, and by deeds one becomes a brahmin. The Dhammapada's last chapter is built on that idea. It opens with courage: cut off the stream of craving, be bold, drive away desire. When you understand how things come to an end, it says, you know the unmade. Then a verse about light. The sun shines by day, the moon by night, the warrior in armor, the brahmana in meditation; but the Buddha shines day and night. And a verse full of wordplay: one is called a brahmana for having put evil away, a samana, a renunciant, for living in calm, and a pabbajita, one gone forth, for sending his own impurities away. The refrain runs through all four days of this chapter: him I call a brahmana. Each verse fills it with conduct: patience, gentleness, truth, freedom from clinging. Nobility, in this chapter, is something you do.

Brahmana. In the Buddha's world a priestly class by birth; in this chapter, a title earned only by conduct.
Your line: nobility is something you do. Birth hands out names; deeds earn them. See you tomorrow.

226.title: Not by matted hair (391–400)
226.hook: not matted hair nor family makes one noble, but truth and goodness; the one who owns nothing and clings to nothing
226.howItsDone: Buddhist monastics wear a simple robe and shave their heads, and teachers often use these verses to warn that the robe itself is not the practice; the rag-robe ideal lives on in some forest traditions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, brahmana, a title earned by conduct, and your line: nobility is something you do.

Everyone wears badges. A uniform, a lanyard, a ring, the right sneakers, the reading list on the coffee table. Spiritual life has them too: beads on the wrist, the right vocabulary, a meditation app streak you'd rather people noticed. In the Buddha's India, some holy men wore theirs as hair grown long and matted, and a robe of animal skin. Today's verses look straight at the badge.
screen: `EVERYONE WEARS BADGES.` → `SPIRITUAL LIFE HAS THEM TOO.` → `LONG, MATTED HAIR.`

segments.voice: Verse three hundred ninety-three, in Max Müller's English: "A man does not become a Brahmana by his platted hair, by his family, or by birth; in whom there is truth and righteousness, he is blessed, he is a Brahmana." Platted, or matted, hair was the sign of a certain kind of ascetic in ancient India, many of them devoted, serious people. The verse isn't mocking them. It's saying the sign isn't the thing. The next verse says it more sharply, to someone vain about his look: what use is your matted hair, what use your robe of goatskin? The inside is a tangle, and you're polishing the outside. Then the real thing, and the picture is surprising. The one this chapter honors might wear rags from a rubbish heap, be thin enough that you can see the veins, and sit alone in the forest, meditating. No badge at all. One verse plays on how people spoke. A man may be born to the right mother and greet others with the polite 'sir' of his class, but if he owns and clings to plenty, that doesn't make him a brahmana. The brahmana owns nothing and clings to nothing. The portrait keeps filling in: the one who has cut every fetter and trembles at nothing; who bears insults, blows and even chains without anger, whose patience is an army; free of anger, faithful in duty, keeping the precepts, tamed. The book has said this before, about the robe, the shaved head and gray hair. Now it says it about the matted hair. The sign isn't the point. The heart is.

227.title: Water on a lotus leaf (401–410)
227.hook: like water on a lotus leaf, like a mustard seed on a needle's point, pleasures don't cling
227.carry: in the water, not soaked by it
227.howItsDone: The lotus is a familiar symbol in Buddhist art, often shown beneath the Buddha's seat; teachers use the water-on-a-lotus-leaf image for living in the world without clinging to it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jaṭā, and your line: not by the hair. The sign isn't the thing.

Watch rain fall on a lotus pond and you'll see something a little magical. The drops land on the broad green leaves and don't soak in. They bead up into bright little balls, roll around, and slide off, leaving the leaf completely dry. Scientists have a name for it now, the lotus effect, and they've studied the leaf's tiny waxy bumps to make self-cleaning surfaces. Buddhists noticed it much earlier, and saw in it a picture of a free mind.
screen: `RAIN ON A LOTUS POND.` → `THE DROPS BEAD UP AND ROLL OFF.` → `THE LEAF STAYS DRY.`

segments.voice: Verse four hundred one, in Max Müller's English: "Him I call indeed a Brahmana who does not cling to pleasures, like water on a lotus leaf, like a mustard seed on the point of a needle." Two pictures. The water rolls off the leaf. And a mustard seed, tiny and round, can't balance on a needle's point; it just drops. Notice what the verse doesn't say. It doesn't say the rain never falls, or that pleasure never touches this person. The lotus lives in the pond. The rain lands. Pleasant things arrive and are enjoyed, and they don't soak in and take hold. A few verses later the mustard seed returns: passion, hatred, pride and scorn have dropped away like a mustard seed from a needle's point. The portrait keeps growing. The one who has put down the burden. The one of deep wisdom who knows the right road from the wrong. The one who has laid down the rod toward every living being, weak or strong, and neither kills nor causes killing. Gentle among the violent, calm among the grasping. Speech true, useful and never harsh. Taking nothing that isn't given, long or short, large or small, good or bad. On this third brahmana day you can hear the book gathering everything it has taught: harmlessness, patience, true speech, not taking, not clinging. And the lotus, which grew from a rubbish heap back in chapter four, returns as the picture of the whole thing: in the water, not soaked by it.

Enjoy it for a breath, then watch it bead up and roll gently off into the pond, nothing lost, nothing clinging. If another drop comes, let it fall and roll off too, and rest as the leaf.
Paduma. The lotus: pleasures land and are enjoyed, then roll off like water on its leaf; they don't soak in and take hold.
Your line: in the water, not soaked by it. Pleasure lands; it doesn't have to take hold. Until tomorrow.

228.title: The end of the path (411–423)
228.hook: the one gone beyond both good and evil ties, bright as the moon, who has reached the end
228.howItsDone: In Theravada tradition the brahmana chapter is read as a portrait of the arahant, one who has reached the end of the path; monks often chant the Dhammapada in full at special occasions, and many lay Buddhists read it through more than once.

segments.voice: Yesterday, paduma, and your line: in the water, not soaked by it. Today, the last verses of the book.
screen: `PADUMA — IN THE WATER, NOT SOAKED BY IT.`

segments.voice: The last page of a long book has its own feeling. You slow down. You read the final lines twice. Part of you wants it to go on, and part of you is proud you're here at all. Seventy-one days ago you opened the Dhammapada, and its first verse said: the mind comes first. Today come its last thirteen verses, four hundred eleven to four hundred twenty-three, and the book closes. It ends, fittingly, with a portrait of someone who has arrived.
screen: `THE LAST PAGE OF A LONG BOOK.` → `SEVENTY-ONE DAYS AGO: THE MIND FIRST.` → `A PORTRAIT OF ARRIVAL.`

segments.voice: The last verses finish the portrait of the brahmana, the one who has reached the end: no longings left, no doubts, the deathless touched. Then a surprising line: this one has gone beyond both good and evil, beyond the ties of both. It doesn't mean he stopped caring about goodness. The tradition reads it as going beyond the pull of both kinds of karma, good and bad, the fuel that keeps the wheel of rebirth turning. He is free of grief and stain, and the next verse compares him to the moon: bright, clear, serene, undisturbed. Then pictures you'll recognize. He has crossed the muddy, difficult road of rebirth and reached the far shore. His path can't be traced, the text says, not by gods or spirits or people, like the birds in the sky from chapter seven. He calls nothing his own, before, behind or in between, the words the acrobat Uggasena heard on his pole. And the last verse, four hundred twenty-three, describes the one who remembers his former lives, sees the heavens and the lower states, and has reached the end of births: a sage, complete. That's where the book stops. Not with a rule or a command, but with a picture of freedom. It began with a choice, the mind coming first, and pain following a bad thought like a wheel following an ox. It ends with the wheel standing still. Read it as a promise, a portrait or a direction to walk: you have now read the whole thing, twenty-six chapters, four hundred twenty-three verses.

segments.voice: Let the whole book sit with you, and let a few pictures drift through as they come: the wheel following the ox, the bee and the flower, the deep still lake, the elephant bearing the arrow, the creeper, the emptied boat, the lotus leaf. Don't hold on to any of them; let each one arrive and roll off. Then let the pictures go, and just sit with the breath, at the end of the path.
Pāragū. One gone to the far shore: the book's last portrait is one who has crossed over, bright as the moon, with nothing left to cling to.
Your line: the wheel standing still. Whichever picture comes back on its own is yours. Day two hundred twenty-eight: the book is closed.

229.title: Your ten verses
229.hook: pick the verses that stayed with you
229.howItsDone: Some Buddhists carry a few Dhammapada verses by heart rather than the whole book; teachers often give a single verse as a theme for reflection, and some people keep favorite verses written by a shrine or a desk.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pāragū, and your line: the wheel standing still. Today, graduation week.

Some songs nobody ever sits down to memorize. They just stick, because at some point they meant something, and they come back at odd moments: in the shower, in the car, on a hard day. A book of verses can work the same way. You've read four hundred twenty-three of them. Many will blur. A handful may already have stuck, and those tend to come back when they're needed. Today is for finding them.
screen: `SONGS YOU KNOW BY HEART.` → `THEY JUST STUCK.` → `A HANDFUL MAY HAVE STUCK.`

segments.voice: The Dhammapada was made to be carried this way. Tradition says the Buddha's teachings were passed on by heart long before they were written down, and a verse can still travel that way: learned as a child, heard in a teacher's talk, chanted at a festival. Monks might learn the whole book by heart; a grandmother might know six verses and live by them. Both count. Here's a way to find yours. First, walk back through the book in your mind. The twin verses: the mind comes first. Verse five, in Max Müller's English: "For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love, this is an old rule." Earnestness, and the island no flood can overwhelm. The fletcher straightening the arrow. The bee that takes nectar and leaves the flower. The spoon that never tastes the soup. The deep, still lake. Conquering yourself, rather than a thousand times a thousand in battle. Drop by drop, the water pot fills. The world seen as a bubble. Not to do evil, to do good, to purify the mind: the teaching of all the Buddhas. Overcoming anger by not-anger. The Buddhas only point the way. The forest, the elephant, the creeper, the emptied boat, the lotus leaf. Second, notice which ones tug at you: not the ones you think you ought to pick, the ones that came back on some ordinary day. Third, write them down, in your own words if you like. There's no right list. Two people who read the same book will choose different verses, because they're living different lives. A verse becomes yours when it has a job in your life.

230.title: The Dhammapada in the world
230.hook: carried across Asia in Pali, Gandhari, Sanskrit and Chinese; Max Müller brought it into English in 1870
230.howItsDone: The Pali Dhammapada is chanted and studied throughout Theravada Buddhism; related collections were kept by other early schools, and Tibetan and East Asian Buddhists know the sayings through the Udanavarga and Chinese versions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dhammapada, and your line: yours. A verse becomes yours when it has a job in your life.

In the eighteen nineties, in the desert near Khotan, on the old Silk Road in what is now western China, a French expedition came away with pieces of a very old manuscript. Birch bark, in a script few people could read, in a language of the old northwest of India. When scholars finally worked it out, they found verses they knew. Far from where the Pali canon was kept, someone had carried the same sayings you've been reading.
screen: `BIRCH BARK NEAR KHOTAN.` → `A SCRIPT FEW COULD READ.` → `VERSES THEY KNEW.`

segments.voice: The version you've read is the Pali Dhammapada, kept by the Theravada tradition of Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia. But it has cousins. That birch-bark manuscript is the Gandhari Dharmapada, named after Gandhara, the region of today's northern Pakistan and eastern Afghanistan where its language was spoken. Another version survives in a mixed Indian language and is named after the city of Patna. A larger Sanskrit collection, the Udanavarga, used by other early schools, shares many verses with it and was later translated into Tibetan. And the sayings went into Chinese early, in the third century, and were read in monasteries. The collections don't match exactly: chapters are arranged differently, some verses are missing, some are added. What's striking is how much stays the same across languages and centuries: hatred ending by not-hatred, the mind coming first, the bee and the flower. Then the verses traveled west. A Danish scholar, Viggo Fausböll, published the Pali text in Europe with a Latin translation in the eighteen fifties. Max Müller brought it into English in eighteen seventy and revised it in eighteen eighty-one for the Sacred Books of the East, the version you've read. Many more translations have followed, and the book is still read by Buddhists and by people of other paths. Each of them carried it: monks memorizing on foot, scribes on birch bark, translators at desks. And now you, if you pass one verse along.
screen: `THE PALI, AND ITS COUSINS.` · `GANDHARI, PATNA, SANSKRIT, CHINESE.` · `SO MUCH STAYS THE SAME.` · `FAUSBÖLL, THEN MÜLLER, 1870.` · then, large: `WHO ELSE CARRIED IT.`

231.title: Camp 4 close: you read it
231.hook: 26 chapters, 423 verses: one whole book of the Buddha's sayings
231.howItsDone: In Theravada countries, reading or chanting the whole Dhammapada is a respected practice, some monastic students memorize it, and lay Buddhists return to it through their lives, reading a verse or a chapter at a time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gandhari Dharmapada, and your line: who else carried it. Today, the end of the week, and the last day of camp four.

A copy of the Dhammapada can sit on a shelf for years, next to the other books someone means to read someday. A verse from it turns up on a poster, or a verse that was never in it at all. Reading the whole thing, in order, first verse to last, is a different matter. Seventy-four days ago, camp four began with a promise: all twenty-six chapters, all four hundred twenty-three verses, a few a day. You kept it.
screen: `A COPY ON THE SHELF.` → `A VERSE ON A POSTER.` → `SEVENTY-FIVE DAYS, KEPT.`

segments.voice: The camp's words. Dhammapada: dhamma, the teaching, and pada, a step, a path, a line of verse. Appamada: earnestness, heedfulness, the path to the deathless. Citta: the mind, trembling like a fish on dry land, straightened like an arrow. Pandita: the wise one; someone who points out your faults is like a guide to buried treasure. Arahant: the one whose path, like a bird's in the sky, can't be traced. Tanha: thirst, the creeper that grows while no one watches. Bhikkhu: the monk who lives on what is given, restrained in every sense. And brahmana: a title earned not by birth, but by conduct. Around those words, twenty-six chapters of pictures: the wheel following the ox, the island no flood can overwhelm, the spoon and the soup, the deep lake, the broken gong, the yellow leaf, the forest, the elephant, the emptied boat, the lotus leaf. Not a summary, not a quote on a mug: the book itself, in its own order. And it ends where it began. Verse one, in Max Müller's English: "All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts." Heard after four hundred twenty-two more verses, it may sound different. By now the book has shown what it means by thought: the mind that can be guarded, trained, emptied, and set free. Tomorrow camp five begins: the depths. It opens with four rooms the Buddha said a person can live in: kindness, compassion, joy for others, and equanimity. Then the foundations of mindfulness, the Heart Sutra, the koans, and more.
screen: `EIGHT WORDS, DHAMMAPADA TO BRAHMANA.` · `TWENTY-SIX CHAPTERS OF PICTURES.` · `THE BOOK ITSELF, IN ITS OWN ORDER.` · `VERSE ONE, HEARD AGAIN.` · then, large: `YOU ACTUALLY READ IT.`

segments.voice: You met verse one about ten weeks ago; let it come back now, slowly, one phrase per breath: all that we are, is the result of what we have thought, founded on our thoughts, made up of our thoughts. Then let the words go and watch the thoughts themselves for a while, arriving and leaving, the raw material the whole book was about. No need to change them; just see them.
Appamada. Earnestness, heedfulness, the path to the deathless: today the book closes, twenty-six chapters, four hundred twenty-three verses, one whole book of the Buddha's sayings, read in order.
Your line: you actually read it. All of it, every verse, in order. Camp four, complete.
